# Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)

**When the stock is high and stable (roughly the same as last season) and other boats are taking their sustainable share or below, I take 15–25% above the sustainable share.** The regrowth absorbs the deficit and I bank extra fish each season at minimal cost. In practice, if sustainable is 6.2, I take around 7–7.5.

**When the stock has dropped sharply (e.g., others overfished), I immediately recalibrate to the new sustainable share of the reduced stock.** I do not try to "make up" lost fish by overfishing a diminished stock; that accelerates the decline and shrinks every future season.

**When I observe other boats consistently taking more than the sustainable share, I pull back to the sustainable share or slightly below.** I let them deplete the stock while I conserve my option value in later seasons. This worked well: by holding at or below sustainable while others overfished, the stock stabilized and I was in a strong position for the final push.

**When I observe other boats consistently taking less than the sustainable share, I can afford to take 25–40% above sustainable.** The stock will hold or grow, giving me room to extract extra without long-term cost.

**In the final season, I take a large share but I estimate what the other boats will also take and ensure the total stays under the current stock.** My safe upper bound is: current stock minus my estimate of the other boats' combined catch. If I think the other boats will also go aggressive (which they likely will, since it's the last season), I target roughly 40–50% of the stock divided by the number of boats, not a fixed fraction of the whole stock. Taking too much risks the total exceeding the stock, which can reduce or zero out my catch. In practice: if stock is S and N boats, I take roughly 0.4–0.5 × S/N rather than a bare fraction of S.

**I track the gap between the stock's actual trajectory and the sustainable trajectory each season.** If the stock is declining despite my taking the sustainable share, others are overfishing and I should stay at or below sustainable. If the stock is stable or growing while I take above sustainable, I have room to push a bit higher.

**I never submit a catch that I believe, combined with the other boats' likely catches, will drive the stock to zero.** A zero stock ends everything and may zero out my current catch as well.

**In early seasons with no information on other boats, I take a modest amount above sustainable (10–15%)** to bank some advantage while gathering data on how aggressively the others play.

# Playbook

**Final season:** This is where you win. Calculate how much stock remains after subtracting what others are *likely* to take (use their recent 2–3 season average). Take the large majority of what's left for you — not 40% of total stock, but 70–80% of your *available* share after their expected catches. The only real constraint is not exceeding the stock itself. Do not hover near the sustainable share. A healthy stock in the final season is an asset to be harvested, not preserved.

**Earlier seasons, stock at or above 60:** Take about 1.3–1.6× the stated sustainable share. This banks extra above the cooperative baseline. The regrowth rule (50% of remainder) absorbs moderate overages, especially when stock is high.

**Earlier seasons, stock below 60:** Do NOT reflexively drop to the sustainable share. First check whether the decline is caused by others overfishing or by your own earlier premium. If others are taking near or below sustainable (i.e., they're cooperative), the stock is stable and you can continue taking a 1.3–1.5× premium safely. Only drop toward the sustainable share if *others* are clearly driving the decline and you need to signal restraint to keep them in the cooperative band.

**If the stock is near 100 (carrying capacity):** Push toward the upper end of your range (1.5× or slightly above). Regrowth from a high stock is generous.

**Read the other boats:** If prior seasons show others consistently well above sustainable, do not try to "save" the stock by dropping to the sustainable share yourself — the stock will decline regardless. Match their level or go slightly above it, and rely on the final-season harvest for your big gain. If others are cooperative (near or below sustainable), your premium is safe even at lower stock levels.

**Do not** take the exact sustainable share as a reflex. It is a floor, not a target. Taking it exactly signals no intent to extract surplus and leaves value on the table every season.

**Do not** be timid in the last season. The main way to lose points is staying near sustainable because "the stock looks healthy." Calculate your available share and take most of it.

**Track your cumulative total:** Keep a running tally of what you've landed. In the final season, your remaining target is whatever you need to maximize your total, not some fixed fraction of the stock.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**Core principle:** Your score is only your own total. The stock is a shared resource, but your objective is not to keep it high—it's to maximize what you pull out across all seasons. The "sustainable share" is the amount that keeps the stock flat; it is a reference point, not a ceiling.

**Final season:** Request the full current stock. Do not subtract an estimate of others' catches. In any allocation mechanism (proportional or cap-based), requesting more in the last round is weakly dominant: if total requests exceed the stock you get a proportional share that scales with your request, and if they don't you simply get more. Requesting "stock minus a guess" leaves value on the table for no benefit. In my last episode I requested 35 out of 50.1 available and received only ~26; requesting 50.1 would have yielded a strictly larger share.

**Early seasons (first third):** Take 1.5× to 2× the sustainable share. The stock starts high and has a large buffer. This builds my total while the fishery is resilient. Avoid exceeding 2.5× sustainable early.

**Middle seasons:** Take 1.2× to 1.5× the sustainable share as a default. The purpose of the middle is not to "protect" the stock at all costs—it's to collect fish while still leaving enough for a meaningful final grab. The final-season grab is large but not infinitely large; a 10-unit increase in middle-season collection is worth more than the 3–4 units I might lose from a smaller final grab. Only drop to or below sustainable if the stock is dropping sharply (more than ~30% in a single season) AND there are 3+ seasons remaining.

**When the stock is declining:** Calibrate your response to the rate of decline. A 15–20% drop over one season is normal early-game dynamics and does not warrant cutting below sustainable. A 30%+ drop, or a stock falling below ~40% of its initial value with 3+ seasons left, is a signal to tighten to sustainable or just below. Do not overreact to a single season's drop, especially if it was partly caused by your own earlier above-sustainable plays.

**When I see others catching well below sustainable:** I have room to push. Take 1.5× to 2× sustainable. The stock will hold.

**When I see others catching well above sustainable:** Tighten to 1× sustainable or just below. Avoid being the marginal boat that pushes the stock to zero and forfeits my remaining seasons.

**General rule of thumb for how much above sustainable is safe:** Each unit above sustainable costs roughly 1.5 units of stock (before regrowth). Over the remaining seasons, I should not let the projected stock drop below about 25% of the initial stock before the final round. Below that, my final grab is small enough that the middle-season conservation has paid off. Above that, I'm over-conserving.

**Tracking others:** I watch the trend in others' catches, not just the stock level. If others are consistently pulling back (e.g., dropping from 2× to 1× sustainable over two seasons), the stock will stabilize and I can safely increase my own take. If others are ramping up, I tighten.
